videos.title: Why allocate costs?
videos.take: Allocation serves four purposes; cause-and-effect and benefits received are the best criteria

scenes.say: Allocation can feel arbitrary. But every allocation should serve a purpose and follow a defensible criterion.

scenes.heading: Four purposes
items: Measure income and assets for outsiders
scenes.say: Allocations serve four purposes: to inform economic decisions like pricing; to motivate managers, for example to use a support service carefully; to justify costs or compute reimbursements, as in government contracts; and to measure income and assets for external reporting.

scenes.heading: Criteria for choosing a base
scenes.say: The best criterion is cause and effect: allocate by what drives the cost. When that's not possible, benefits received: who gains most. Fairness is vague, and ability to bear, charging the most profitable units more, distorts decisions.
The purpose decides the method. For decisions, use causal allocations, or leave costs unallocated. For a government contract, follow the contract's rules.
And some costs, like the CEO's salary, have no causal link to any product or customer. For decisions, they're better left unallocated.

scenes.q: Tallgrass charges its most profitable division the largest share of head-office costs because 'it can afford it'. Which criterion is that?
scenes.say: Quick check. Tallgrass charges its most profitable division the most head-office cost, because it can afford it. Which criterion is that? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, ability to bear, the weakest criterion.

videos.title: Allocating corporate costs
videos.take: Allocate corporate cost pools with causal bases, and only as far as the purpose requires

scenes.say: Tallgrass has two divisions and a head office. How should head-office costs be shared?

scenes.heading: Head-office cost pools, 2027
scenes.say: Tallgrass's head office costs $600,000: $200,000 for human resources, $150,000 for I.T., and $250,000 for executives and corporate administration.

scenes.heading: Causal bases
scenes.say: Ana allocates human resources by headcount: sixty employees in Bikes, fifteen in Parts. I.T. by help tickets: twelve hundred and eight hundred. Executive and admin costs have no good causal base, so for decisions she leaves them unallocated.
For other purposes, like long-run pricing or external segment reporting, she might allocate everything, for instance in proportion to revenue. Just be clear which purpose each number serves.

sub: Charge IT by tickets, and divisions
scenes.say: Allocations change behavior. Charging I.T. by help tickets encourages divisions to use the help desk sensibly, but too high a charge might stop them asking for help they need.

scenes.q: HR costs $200,000; Bikes has 60 employees and Parts 15. Bikes' share?
scenes.say: Quick check. HR costs two hundred thousand; Bikes has sixty employees and Parts fifteen. What's Bikes' share? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. Sixty of seventy-five is eighty percent: $160,000.

videos.title: Customer revenues and price discounts
videos.take: Track discounts by customer; list prices hide large differences in what customers actually pay

scenes.say: Customer profitability starts with revenue. And customers rarely pay the list price.

scenes.heading: Trail bike list price $2,400
scenes.say: Three Tallgrass dealers. Prairie Pedals in Sioux Falls buys in volume and gets ten percent off: $2,160 a bike. Lakes Cycle in Brainerd gets five percent. Big Sky Bikes in Bismarck pays full list price.
A price discount is a reduction from list price. Discounts may be earned through volume, negotiated by powerful buyers, or given away by salespeople to close a deal.
If a company records only net revenue, it can't see which customers get which discounts, or whether salespeople are discounting too freely. Tallgrass records list price and discount separately.
But revenue is only half the story. The other half is what each dealer costs to serve.
Quick check. List price twenty-four hundred, discount seven and a half percent. Net price? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The customer cost hierarchy
videos.take: Customer costs occur at output-unit, batch, customer-sustaining, channel and corporate levels

scenes.say: Just as products have a cost hierarchy, so do customers.

scenes.heading: Customer cost hierarchy
scenes.say: Output unit-level costs vary with each bike sold. Batch-level costs vary with orders and deliveries. Customer-sustaining costs support a customer regardless of volume, like sales visits and co-op advertising. Channel costs support a whole channel, like dealers versus online. And corporate-sustaining costs support the whole company.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass's customer activity rates
scenes.say: Ana's activity rates: forty dollars per order, three hundred dollars per truck delivery in Minnesota or four-fifty to the Dakotas, two-fifty per sales visit and a hundred fifty for a rush delivery.
Customer-level analysis assigns costs down to the customer-sustaining level. Channel and corporate costs stay at their own levels.
It's the activity-based logic from Cost Accounting I, applied to customers instead of products.

scenes.q: Co-op advertising paid for one dealer, whatever it buys, is which level?
scenes.say: Quick check. Co-op advertising paid for one dealer, regardless of what it buys, is which level? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Customer-profitability profiles
videos.take: Ranking customers by profit often shows a few earn most of it and some lose money

scenes.say: Put revenue and costs together for each dealer, and the results are often surprising.

scenes.heading: Three dealers, 2027
scenes.say: Prairie Pedals buys two hundred bikes. Despite its discount, it earns $112,000 of gross margin and costs only $10,300 to serve: $101,700 of profit. Lakes Cycle earns $24,100. Big Sky pays full price but orders one bike at a time, far away, with lots of returns. It loses $750.

sub: then falls as loss-makers are added
scenes.say: Plot cumulative profit with customers ranked from most to least profitable, and you often get a whale curve: the best twenty percent of customers may generate more than a hundred percent of profit, with the tail of loss-makers dragging it back down.
Notice the lesson: the discounted customer is the most profitable, and the full-price customer loses money. The cost to serve matters as much as the price.
Managers grasp this best visually: a bar chart of profit by customer, or a cumulative curve, makes the loss-makers obvious.

scenes.q: A dealer: gross margin $30,000; customer-level costs $34,000. Customer-level income?
scenes.say: Quick check. A dealer has thirty thousand of gross margin and thirty-four thousand of customer-level costs. Customer-level income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Acting on customer profitability
videos.take: Change prices, service levels or ordering behavior before dropping a customer; consider lifetime value

scenes.say: Big Sky Bikes loses money. Should Tallgrass drop it? There are better first moves.

scenes.heading: Options for Big Sky
items: Minimum order of 4 bikes per delivery
Reduce sales visits, use video calls
scenes.say: Ana could set a minimum order of four bikes, charge for rush deliveries, combine Big Sky's shipments with other Dakota dealers, and replace some sales visits with video calls.

scenes.heading: Big Sky with changes
scenes.say: With seven orders instead of twenty-five, seven deliveries, four visits, and the same returns and co-op costs, Big Sky earns $9,570 instead of losing $750.

scenes.heading: Before dropping any customer
scenes.say: Before dropping anyone, ask which costs would really disappear, what the customer could become over its lifetime, whether it opens a new territory, and how other dealers would react.
The same analysis works by channel. Tallgrass might find that selling online directly costs less per bike than dealers in some regions, or more once returns and support are counted.

scenes.q: Which is usually the best first step with an unprofitable customer?
opts: Change how the customer is served or priced
scenes.say: Quick check. What's usually the best first step with an unprofitable customer? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Change the cost to serve or the price before dropping anyone.
